verses.1: Al-Mizan presents Sūrah Fuṣṣilat as an early Meccan discourse centred on people's turning from the revealed Qur'an, a turning that entails denial of divine oneness, prophethood, and resurrection; it therefore couples proofs of these principles with promise and warning. The opening calls the Book a tanzīl, ‘sent down,’ from al-Raḥmān, whose encompassing mercy reaches believers and unbelievers, and al-Raḥīm, whose mercy is reserved for believers, thereby indicating its reform of both worldly and afterlife affairs. Its signs are subject to tafṣīl: unlike iḥkām or ijmāl, they are differentiated and brought down as intelligible Arabic speech so that their meanings and purposes can be understood. ‘For a people who know’ may mark the purpose of that Arabic revelation or specify those who understand it; its special concern for Arabs does not limit the Prophet's universal mission, whose public call advanced from relatives and his people to humankind and in fact reached non-Arabs, Jews, and foreign rulers. The Book gives glad tidings and warning, but turning away means refusing to attend to it. Al-Mizan reads the unbelievers' veiled hearts, deaf ears, and intervening curtain as their asserted inability to comprehend, hear, or find common ground with the Prophet's call to divine unity; together they declare his preaching futile. Their ‘So act; we too are acting’ is an implied challenge for each side to prove the other wrong, not a call for each to follow its own faith or to destroy the other. The reply establishes that the Messenger is human like them, with no such barrier between speaker and hearer; his sole distinction is revelation that their worshipworthy God is one. Steadfastness thus means affirming that oneness, negating partners, and seeking forgiveness for past idolatry and sin. The warning against polytheists singles out their refusal of zakat—at this early Meccan point charitable giving to the needy, though tazkiyat al-nafs is also a sound reading if the word bears it—and their denial of the Hereafter, which follows from rejecting resurrection. Believers who work righteousness receive ajr ghayr mamnūn: it may be unending, uncountable, or a freely given reward unmarred by reproach; even their deservingness is itself granted by God. The command concerning creation rebukes disbelief and associating andād, ‘likenesses’ to God in lordship and divinity, despite the manifest ordering of heaven and earth. The distancing force of dhālika magnifies the exalted Lord of all worlds. The earth's two yawm are not twenty-four-hour days but two completed temporal stages of its formation. God then fixed mountains upon the earth, filled it with benefits for plants, animals, and humans, and ordained its provisions. Al-Mizan records readings that make the four days include the earth's first two days, make the two processes parallel, or subsume every listed event in four days; al-Zamakhsharī similarly supplies an implicit total to avoid an apparent eight-day creation against the Qur'an's six-day statements. It judges these readings contrary to the verse's apparent sense: the four days qualify provision alone and denote the four seasons through which sustenance is ordained, not days of creation. ‘Alike for all the seekers’ can mean provisions equal for seekers or their equal distribution, and the seekers include every needy plant, animal, and human. Al-Mizan distinguishes istawāʾ with ilā, ‘turning toward,’ from its use with ʿalā for mastery: God's turning to heaven is creative attention, never movement or change of place. Although some make thumma an order only in narration, it maintains that heaven was created after earth: the other cited sequence concerns the later spreading out, dahw, rather than the earth's initial khalq. Heaven was dukhān, undifferentiated matter which God formed into seven heavens. The command to heaven and earth to come is the creative ‘Be!’ rather than an order to disclose qualities not yet existing. Their exchange is an allegory making creation intelligible, yet also indicates that beings have knowledge and speech suited to their state. It rejects reducing the command to a mere image of irresistible power, since they explicitly choose willing obedience; their intelligent plural form and plural rather than dual wording may express humility among all obedient creatures. Their joint address also indicates an ontological connection and mutual influence in the cosmic order. Al-Mizan explains qaḍāʾ as determining the smoky potentiality into seven heavens in two days. It rejects both the unsupported claim that waḥy here simply means creating heavenly occupants and the reading that it conventionally assigns worship to angels, the latter also conflicting with revelation ‘in’ rather than ‘to’ each heaven. Instead, the heavenly paths are the channels through which the divine command descends from the Lord and is borne successively by the angels inhabiting them to the earth; insofar as God charges those angels with it, that command is His revelation to them. Nothing in the verse establishes that this revelation itself took two days. The lowest heaven is the nearest layered heaven; its lamps are celestial bodies appearing as its adornment, not ornaments spread through all transparent heavens, while the sun and moon illuminate earthly dwellers and its guarding is from devils. The passage's conclusion calls the visible star-and-planet realm the apparent, though not explicit, meaning of the lowest heaven, treats the seven heavens as layered physical realms rather than the celestial bodies themselves, and distinguishes the material bodies subject to terrestrial laws from the heavenly system of angels, commands, gates, and provisions. It finally identifies the angels' seven supernal realms, ʿawālim malakūtiyya, as what the Qur'an calls the seven heavens, using familiar heavens to make their loftiness and role comprehensible.

verses.5: Al-Mizan explains the unbelievers' ‘veils’ as hearts so enclosed that the Prophet's call to divine unity cannot enter or be understood; their deafness and the curtain between them likewise claim that they cannot hear him or reach agreement with him. Together these images tell the Prophet to abandon hope of persuading them. ‘So act; we too are acting’ is consequently an implied threat: each side is to do what it can to prove the other wrong. The commentary rejects readings that make it a call for each party to follow its own faith or for each to seek the other's destruction, because neither is the apparent sense.
verses.6: Al-Mizan reads the reply as denying that any barrier separates the Messenger from his hearers: he is human like them, associates and speaks with them as they do, and is not an angelic being whose words could not reach their hearts or ears. His only distinction is revelation that their worshipworthy God is one, not many. Being steadfast toward Him therefore requires affirming His oneness, rejecting partners, and seeking forgiveness for prior idolatry and sins. The woe addresses idolaters marked by failure to give zakat and by denial of the Hereafter. Here zakat means charitable giving to the poor and needy, since obligatory almsgiving had not yet been legislated in this early Meccan period; the commentary accepts purification of the soul, tazkiyat al-nafs, as a reading only if zakat can bear that meaning. Their separate description as disbelievers in the Hereafter stresses that denial of resurrection defines them.

verses.8: Al-Mizan gives three possible senses for ajr ghayr mamnūn, the reward of faithful people who do righteous deeds: it may be unending, uncountable, or given without the reproach and condescension of mann. The last reading suits its being called a reward, since faith and righteous deeds make them deserving of it; yet even that deservingness is ultimately God's gift, not something they gave themselves.
verses.9: Al-Mizan takes the question as an astonished rebuke: after the manifest signs of God's oneness in creating and directing heaven and earth, it is beyond belief that people should disbelieve or associate andād, ‘likenesses,’ with Him in lordship and divinity. The emphatic Arabic makes the amazement explicit, and the distancing pronoun in ‘That is the Lord of all worlds’ magnifies His exaltation above such delusions; as director of all affairs, He can have no rival lord or god. The two ‘days’ are not terrestrial twenty-four-hour days but two periods in which the earth's creation was completed, indicating two distinct stages of formation.
verses.10: Al-Mizan links this verse to the question about the earth's two-day creation: God fixed mountains upon the earth, blessed it with benefits for every living inhabitant, and ordained its sustenance. Rawāsi denotes fixed mountains, and every feminine singular pronoun in the verse returns to the earth. It records three readings of ‘in four days’: that the four include the earth's original two days; that creation and provision occurred in parallel over four; or that all the listed acts occupy four, a reading requiring much implicit material. Al-Zamakhsharī likewise supplies an implicit total—two days for earth and two for its provisions—because otherwise commentators find an eight-day total when the heavens take two days, contrary to the Qur'an's recurrent six-day creation statement. Al-Mizan nevertheless judges that reconciliation contrary to the apparent wording. The four days qualify only the ordaining of provisions and are the four seasons produced by the sun's changing position, not days of creating provisions. Creation of earth and the fashioning of the smoky heavens into seven heavens take four days in these verses; the days of provision concern their ordination rather than creation, so the Qur'an's six-day formula concerns creation and excludes the ordering of affairs. ‘Alike for all the seekers’ may either be an absolute expression of provisions being equal for seekers or qualify the provisions as fairly apportioned so that each is sufficed. The seekers are plants, animals, and humans: all seek by their need for sustenance, not only by conscious request.
verses.11: Al-Mizan distinguishes istawāʾ governed by ilā, ‘turning toward,’ from its use with ʿalā for taking mastery: here God turns to heaven in the sense of creating it, not by moving from place to place, for He transcends place. Karh is externally imposed difficulty, unlike kurh, which arises within a person. Thumma therefore indicates that the heavens were created after earth, not merely a later stage in the Qur'anic narration. The proposed contrary sequence concerns the later spreading out, dahw, of earth—with its water, pastures, and mountains—not its initial khalq; ‘after that’ there is even clearer temporal language. The heaven was dukhān, pure undifferentiated matter, which God formed into seven heavens, hence the initial singular samāʾ rather than samāwāt. Al-Mizan takes ‘Come, willingly or unwillingly’ as the creative command, like ‘Be!,’ rather than an instruction to reveal latent qualities before the heavens existed. The dialogue is an allegorical rendering of creation for ordinary understanding, but also discloses that entities have a degree of knowledge and may be given speech appropriate to their condition, enabling divine address. It rejects treating the words as only a figure for irresistible power, since heaven and earth answer that they choose to come willingly. Their intelligent plural tāʾiʿīn suits an address and response; their use of the plural rather than dual may humbly count them among God's obedient creatures. Their joint command and answer, despite separate accounts of their creation and management, further indicate an ontological connection through which parts of the cosmos affect one another.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains qaḍāʾ here as determining the formerly smoky, unformed potentiality into seven heavens in two days; the feminine plural pronoun refers to the heavens. An alternative makes qaḍāʾ simply ‘make,’ but the passage does not pursue other grammatical proposals. The verse and its predecessor clarify what is left ambiguous in the account of heaven and earth once interwoven and then unravelled. It records the view that waḥy, ‘revelation,’ means creating each heaven's capacities and occupants, and the view that it conventionally gives angels their prescribed worship. The first and its claimed simultaneity need clear proof; the second conflicts with revelation occurring ‘in’ each heaven rather than ‘to’ it. Reading ‘its ordinance’ as merely what God wanted reduces to one of those two alternatives. Al-Mizan instead derives a subtler account from verses about the divine command: the heavens are the origin and successive paths through which the command descends to earth, borne by the angels who inhabit them. If amr is the creative command, al-amr al-takwīnī, that makes things exist by ‘Be!,’ these passages show angels carrying it from the Lord through one heaven after another until it reaches the terrestrial realm. Insofar as God charges each class of angels with bearing it, that command is His revelation to them; thus ‘He revealed in each heaven its ordinance’ means that each heaven's angels receive the command assigned to them. The text supplies no evidence that this revelation took the same two days as the seven heavens' formation. Al-Mizan takes the lowest heaven, dunyā, to be nearest earth in a layered arrangement. Its lamps are celestial bodies, seen as its adornment; if bodies were distributed through transparent heavens without obstruction, they would ornament all rather than the one named. The sun and moon are lights in relation to earthly inhabitants, and its guarding is against devils. The closing formula marks the sublime order of this arrangement. The conclusion says the apparent, though not explicit, sense places the stars and planets in the nearest heaven; the seven heavens are layered physical realms, not the celestial bodies themselves, and the other six are undescribed beyond their layers. Yet the angelic abodes, their descent and ascent with commands and records, heavenly gates, and descending provisions belong to a system fundamentally distinct from material bodies governed by terrestrial physical laws. The commentary therefore identifies the angels' seven supernal realms, ʿawālim malakūtiyya, as the seven heavens, described through the visible heavens to make their loftiness and function intelligible.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains ṣāʿiqa as a thunderbolt whose classifications as death, punishment, or natural fire describe its effects, not different realities: it is a tremendous explosion of the air. Here it corresponds to the punishments of ʿĀd and Thamūd, respectively described as a wind and a cry. The past tense in andhartukum, ‘I warn you,’ signifies that the threatened event is certain.
verses.14: Al-Mizan presents this verse as the context for the thunderbolt of ʿĀd and Thamūd. Its plural ‘messengers’ does not mean that Hūd and Ṣāliḥ alone are called a plural: every messenger bears the one summons, so the sending or denial of one is in effect the sending or denial of all. ‘Before them and behind them’ means from every direction, or past and present: the call to monotheism was made privately and publicly, individually and collectively, through promise and warning. Their demand for angels rejects the possibility of human prophethood; from it they conclude that God neither wished nor sent the message, and so reject its monotheistic content.
verses.15: Al-Mizan says that the people of ʿĀd’s arrogance was necessarily bi ghayr al-ḥaqq, since arrogance is inherently undue. It explains rīḥ ṣarṣar as variously an intense toxic wind, an extremely cold wind, or a wind whose destructive force was deafening, and ayyām naḥisāt as days of misfortune and misery; one report connects them with blinding dust and the cloud of punishment in (46:24). The gale gave them disgrace in this world, while the Hereafter’s punishment is still more disgraceful. Their being ‘not helped’ excludes both saviour and intercessor.

verses.17: Al-Mizan reads Thamūd’s guidance as being shown the right path, taught its realities in faith and practice, and enabled to distinguish it from error. Their preferred blindness is therefore ḍalāla chosen over hudā, with the metaphor implying that guidance is sight and error blindness. The literal phrase ʿadhāb hūn intensifies the humiliation of the punishment: after receiving that clarification, they chose error and were seized by the cry as recompense for what they earned.
verses.18: Al-Mizan takes the continuous form wa kānū yattaqūn to show that the saved people combined faith with sustained Godwariness and righteous deeds; this was why they escaped annihilating punishment. It considers the verse a conclusion to both the accounts of ʿĀd and Thamūd, rather than only the latter as most commentators maintain.
verses.19: Al-Mizan defines ḥashr as forcibly driving a group from its homes, and says that holding them in check means restraining those in front until the rest join them. One reading takes their march ‘toward the Fire’ as the Resurrection and judgment, with the Fire named for their final destination; the ensuing testimony of their limbs supports this. Another takes it as their actual dispatch to hell, allowing a second testimony at its brink. It also reports that ‘the enemies of Allah’ may specifically be the idolaters among the Prophet’s people, as indicated by (41:25), rather than all disbelievers.
verses.20: Al-Mizan holds that the limbs’ testimony is genuine recounting of sins they perceived in worldly life, which entails that they already possessed awareness; a knowledge or voice newly created for them on the Day of Judgment, or a merely figurative ‘testimony,’ would not be actual witness or conclusive proof against a denier. Hearing and sight can testify to what they perceived even where they did not participate—for example, hearing divine signs or blasphemy, or seeing signs or prohibited conduct—while the skin testifies to sins in which touch participated. ‘Skins’ apparently means the whole skin and embraces forbidden enjoyments such as fornication; it may also include the testimony of hands and feet. The reported restriction of skins to private parts is a possible polite allusion.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains the sinners’ address to their skins either as shocked inquiry, since the skin participated directly in the sins whereas sight and hearing observed them, or as further reviling of them, especially if skin alludes to private parts. It insists that qawl, takallum, nuṭq and shahāda retain their literal sense: the limbs genuinely speak what they previously knew. God compels their truthful disclosure, but that neither weakens their credibility nor removes its force against their owners. Their answer that God gave speech to all things means that the capacity is not unique to these limbs; creation and return also show that God, the ever-rightful owner of their existence and acts, already knows what they disclose.

Al-Mizan rejects readings that make the speech newly created on the Day, mere sounds, or a figure for their condition, as well as restrictions of ‘all things’ to living speakers or reductions of their speech to bare signification. Those readings assume, without warrant, that non-human or inanimate things lack knowledge and real speech. It argues from Qur’anic descriptions of universal praise, the heaven and earth’s answer, idols’ hostility, the earth’s report, and bodily testimony that all existents have knowledge and volition, though their kinds and effects need not resemble human awareness; the intelligent behaviour of plants and natural phenomena illustrates this possibility.

The commentary’s philosophical excursus defines knowledge as the presence of one thing to another and as immaterial existence: knowing agents and objects of knowledge are therefore immaterial, while matter, as matter, neither knows nor is known. Yet material things have a subsisting aspect not subject to their continual change; through that immaterial aspect, they can know as do entities of the intelligible and imaginal planes.
verses.22: Al-Mizan grounds the rebuke in God’s universal creatorship and witnessing: no creature, deed, limb, instrument, or circumstance can hide anything from Him. The sinners did not conceal themselves while disobeying because they thought their limbs unaware; rather, with lākin meaning ‘no, rather,’ they made light of God’s witnessing and supposed that He did not know most particulars of their deeds, even if they acknowledged His general knowledge. The rebuke may address idolaters particularly or sinners generally. Their limbs’ testimony is consequently an extension of God’s own witnessing, not an independent limit upon it.
verses.23: Al-Mizan explains ardākum as ruin or perishing and gives two grammatical readings. On the first, their supposition is set against direct knowledge and witnessing: it avails nothing against truth, destroys them, and makes them losers. On the second, the verse identifies the specific supposition—that God did not know most of their deeds—as what made sin seem trivial, led to ingratitude, and thus ruined them.
verses.24: Al-Mizan defines mathwā as a permanent residence and yastaʿtibū as trying to repair an estranged relationship and regain favour. The verse means that the Fire remains their settled abode whether they endure it or seek to make amends and apologise; their excuses will not be accepted and they will not be redeemed.
verses.25: Al-Mizan traces taqyīḍ, ‘assigning,’ to exchange: had they been faithful and Godwary, they would have been supported by guiding companions, but their disbelief and profligacy brought an exchanged companionship of devils as recompense. It notes, but does not prefer, the reading that they were given evil jinn and human companions instead of virtuous associations they had neglected. Their companions make present worldly enjoyments and future ambitions seem fair; this can include sins sent ahead and evil customs left for later people. The proposal that ‘before’ is worldly access and ‘behind’ a denied Hereafter is judged implausible. The word of punishment consequently became due against them, as against prior jinn and human peoples, and their loss also confirms that death applies to jinn.
verses.26: Al-Mizan defines lughuw as baseless or meaningless speech, so the faithless urge one another to drown the Qur’an out with noise. Their demonstrative reference to ‘this Qur’an’ shows that it is their sole concern. The command exposes their inability either to rival its discourse or refute it persuasively: they seek to disrupt the Prophet’s recitation, prevent people hearing its message, and blunt its social effect.
verses.27: Al-Mizan takes the promised severe punishment, in context, to concern those who ordered people not to listen to the Qur’an, although the wording is general. ‘The worst of what they used to do’ may mean all their misdeeds, or only their gravest crimes; the latter reading intensifies the warning and deters similar conduct.
verses.28: Al-Mizan treats the Fire as an explanatory apposition, predicate, or the subject of the following clause, while the grammatical phrase ‘as a requital’ may depend on an implicit verb or on the stated requital. The substantive meaning is that the Fire will encompass the enemies of God, each having an everlasting dwelling within it, as recompense for impugning the divine signs.
verses.29: Al-Mizan says that, in Hell, the faithless will ask to be shown the jinn and humans whom they followed into error. They want to trample them in order to abase them, increase their punishment, and make them among the lowest.
verses.30: Al-Mizan understands istiqāma as adhering without deviation to the straight path and remaining steadfast in one’s professed belief. The verses therefore shift from the faithless’ fate to the faithful’s pleasant Hereafter. The angels descend to comfort them: fear concerns expected loss or punishment, while grief concerns loss or regret already incurred; their reassurance means that sins are forgiven and punishment is averted. Their promise of paradise is delivered after the faithful have left worldly life, where that promise was first received.
verses.31:
Al-Mizan reads the angels’ friendship in the Hereafter as continuous with, and resulting from, their friendship with the faithful in worldly life. This does not compete with God’s walāya, since angels are intermediaries of His mercy and possess no independent existence; the contrast with the devils assigned to God’s enemies shows that these guiding angels support those who have God’s friendship. It distinguishes them from guardian angels and angels appointed over provision and death, who attend faithful and faithless alike, and reports that some instead take the speech as God’s.

In the Hereafter, ‘whatever your souls desire’ includes every enjoyment, while ‘whatever you ask for’ is broader because requests can exceed desire. Thus the faithful receive all they desire and more: whatever they ask is granted as hospitality from the All-forgiving, All-merciful.

verses.33: Al-Mizan contrasts the faithless’ effort to silence the Qur’an with God’s reassurance that the Prophet’s summons is the best speech. Though the wording includes every caller to God, it is qualified: righteous action manifests noble intention, and professing submission ensures that the caller believes and adheres to the message rather than pursuing a corrupt aim. ‘Speech’ here means belief or opinion. The Prophet is the archetype for callers to God, and the verse instructs him in the most effective invitation to affect souls before directing him to the inequality of good and evil.
verses.34: Al-Mizan says that good and evil qualities differ in their effects on souls. ‘Respond with what is best’ means answering each evil with its superior contrary—truth for falsehood, good sense for ignorance and immoderation, and forbearance for wrongdoing—rather than another evil. It promises that this response can transform one between whom there was enmity into a sympathetic friend. The fuller phrase about existing enmity is deliberately more eloquent than simply saying ‘enemy.’
verses.35: Al-Mizan treats this as emphatic praise of responding with what is best. It is granted only to those endowed with human perfection and good character, and that great endowment belongs exclusively to those who practise ṣabr, patience.
verses.36: Al-Mizan defines nazgh as a goad that drives an animal. The tempter is most aptly Satan himself, since the Prophet cannot be tempted by waswās; alternatively, it is Satan’s suggestions to hostile followers, goading them to harass the Prophet, for whom responding with what is best is ineffective. On that alternative, the address to the Prophet is indirect instruction for the faithful generally. Seeking protection—ʿaudh, ʿiyādh, maʿādh, or istiʿādha—means taking refuge with God from this goading, because He hears their plea or speech and knows their state or deeds.
verses.37: Al-Mizan says that the ordered night, day, sun, and moon are signs whose unity indicates the oneness of their creating and directing Lord, and thus the necessity of worshipping Him alone. Since the sun and moon are created and governed signs, one must not prostrate to them but to their Creator. The pronoun ‘them’ includes all four signs, and the conditional phrase shows that worship of God cannot be combined with worship of another.
verses.38: Al-Mizan identifies those near the Lord as angels wholly devoted to worship. Their glorification is ‘for Him’ alone, and ‘night and day’ expresses its unceasing constancy, not temporal succession for angels. Thus, even if disbelievers refuse exclusive prostration, the angels with the Lord worship and glorify Him without weariness.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains khushūʿ as humbled desolation, ihtizāz as intense movement, and rubūw as growth and rising: rain makes barren earth flourish with plants. The verse likens this to an abject person who acquires what meets his needs and becomes clothed, joyful, and visibly at ease. This transformation is an argument for the Resurrection.
verses.40: Al-Mizan places this verse between the preceding warnings and proofs and the ensuing defence of the Qur’an. Ilḥād, sacrilege or swerving, covers every profanation of divine signs: worshipping created cosmic signs such as the sun and moon, or treating revelation as forgery or the Prophet’s imagining, drowning out the Qur’an, and interpreting it by whim or to create discord. Such people cannot be hidden from God. The contrast admits only the two classes: those cast into the Fire and those who arrive safe through upright faith; no intercession, aid, or accepted excuse awaits the profaners. ‘Act as you wish’ heightens this threat because God sees all that they do.
verses.41:
Al-Mizan identifies al-Dhikr as the Qur’an and, through ‘when it comes to them,’ its defiers as the contemporary Arab idolaters. It takes their predicate most naturally from the preceding verse: rejecting the Qur’an is a form of sacrilege against divine signs and brings the Fire; alternatively, the omitted predicate itself leaves the threatened fate to the audience’s imagination. Al-Zamakhsharī’s report that the phrase is a badal of those who profane the signs supports this reading. Other proposed predicates, including later phrases in the passage, require cumbersome constructions.

The Qur’an is an ʿazīz Book, either without equal or, more aptly here, incapable of being overcome. Falsehood cannot approach it means that no false content can be interpolated into it, and its doctrines, laws, ordinances, ethics and predictions cannot be invalidated. ‘From before it nor from behind it’ can mean from revelation until the Day of Resurrection, or from every direction; either way it excludes alteration and distortion. This inviolability follows from its descent from the All-wise, whose acts are flawless, and the All-laudable.

verses.43: Al-Mizan takes the saying to be the accusations of the Prophet’s disbelieving people—that he is a magician, madman, poet, speaker of nonsense, or seeker of authority—which repeat what earlier peoples said to their messengers. God’s being forgiving and exacting painful retribution then threatens them to consider whether their response merits forgiveness or punishment, for every good and evil deed receives its like. It also reports an alternative reading: that what is ‘said’ means the revelation concerning defiers of the Reminder, which repeats the warning given to earlier messengers.
verses.44:
Al-Mizan explains ʿajamī as unclear, non-eloquent speech, whether or not its speaker is ethnically Arab; calling a discourse ʿajamī or ʿarabī is therefore figurative. Had the Qur’an been unclear and inarticulate, the deniers would have objected that its verses were not set out plainly and that a foreign revelation had been sent to an Arab prophet. Its singular form stresses the contrast between the revelation’s hypothetical language and the Arab character of its addressee, rather than the number of the audience; al-Zamakhsharī’s grammatical illustration likewise makes this contrast, not gender or number, the point.

The commentary says the Qur’an’s effect does not arise from language but from the division between believers and disbelievers. For believers it guides to truth and heals hearts of doubt and uncertainty; for the faithless it becomes deafness and blindness, matching their earlier confession of deaf ears. Being ‘called from a distant place’ is a parable for people who neither hear admonition nor attend to argument.
verses.45: Al-Mizan presents the differing reception of Moses’ Book as consolation to the Prophet for his people’s obstinacy. Judgment was deferred by God’s prior decree that people would have an earthly abode and sustenance for a time (7:24). Moses’ people were in grave doubt about their scripture, just as the Prophet sees doubt among his own people.
verses.46: Al-Mizan says that actions return to their doer: righteous conduct ultimately benefits one’s own soul, while evil and harm to others rebound upon it. Reward and punishment therefore put each thing in its proper place and are not injustice to God’s innumerable servants. The hyperbolic ‘not tyrannical’ rather than merely ‘not unjust’ underscores this complete absence of injustice.
verses.47: Al-Mizan says that knowledge of the Hour belongs to God alone, while every fruit’s emergence and every conception and birth occur with His detailed knowledge. As creator, transformer, knower, and watcher over all things, He alone governs the cosmos and is its Lord and the sole divinity. This is why the idolaters will be asked on that Day where their alleged partners are. They will say that no one among them can testify to, or even see, such partners; the beings they invoked will abandon them, and they will know with certainty that no refuge from punishment exists. The commentary notes readings of the day-clause as qualifying their speech, as an inexpressibly momentous omission, or as an implicit command to remember, and regards the first as most fitting to the argument.

verses.49: Al-Mizan attributes obstinate rejection of evident truth to human delusion. People continually seek what they count as worldly good, but when an irremediable evil removes the means they relied upon, they become hopeless and despondent. This despair does not necessarily exclude simultaneous hope in God.
verses.50: Al-Mizan says that calling restored prosperity God’s ‘mercy’ shows it is a gift He lets a person taste after distress, neither a necessity nor something to which that person has a right. Yet the person forgets the earlier hardship, treats the blessing as private entitlement beyond accountability, denies that the Hour will come, and arrogantly expects the best outcome even if returned to the Lord. This self-entitlement denies the blessing’s merciful source; it parallels the garden-owner’s claim in (18:36). The promise to inform the faithless of their deeds and make them taste harsh punishment is a threat.
verses.51: Al-Mizan explains that turning aside, naʾā bi jānibih, means withdrawing into oneself in pride, while duʿāʾ ʿarīḍ denotes wide, lengthy, incessant supplication. The verse reproves the human being for disregarding God in blessing and remembering Him with persistent prayer only when calamity arrives.
verses.52: Al-Mizan defines extreme defiance as an irreconcilable disagreement and says the oblique ‘someone who’ highlights that trait as the cause of error rather than merely naming the idolaters. If the Qur’an is from God and they disbelieve, none is more astray, for they reject the ultimate truth without reconciliation. Since its claim could be true, rational avoidance of harm requires considering it; turning from it wholesale risks eternal ruin.
verses.53:
Al-Mizan first takes ‘it is the truth’ to mean that the Qur’an is true. The signs in horizons and souls are then its fulfilled predictions: God’s aid to the Prophet and believers, their establishment and victory, and retribution against Quraysh. It illustrates the outward signs through the expansion of the Muslim cause and the inward signs through Quraysh kinsmen’s defeat at Badr; such events are signs because the Qur’an foretold them and they occurred as promised, not merely because victories happen in history.

It also allows a broader reading: God will manifest His religion over all others until only He is worshipped and humankind attains worldly felicity. The first reading is directed to Meccan idolaters and their supporters, the second to the world’s idolaters and human society, and both may hold together. A third reading concerns death, when illusions, false objects of invocation and all means fall away; then ‘it’ is read as ‘He,’ God the Real.

The rhetorical question says that God’s presence with all things is itself sufficient proof: every existent depends on Him in every respect, while He sustains and governs it. Under the first two readings, it both directly proves the Qur’an’s monotheistic content and offers a shorter proof than awaiting fulfilled signs.
verses.54: Al-Mizan says the audience fails to benefit from the clearest proof of divine oneness—God’s witness to all things—because it doubts meeting its Lord, that is, doubts that He is not veiled from creatures by His attributes and acts. God’s encompassing of all things should remove this doubt: in a manner befitting His divinity, no place is empty of Him, yet He is confined to no place and contained by nothing.
